title: The C-Grade Paper That Changed the Constitution
description: A college student received a C on a government term paper about a forgotten 1789 legal loophole. Ten years later, his thesis became the 27th Amendment to the US Constitution. 📜 Do you think modern amendments should have strict expiration dates?
script:
Imagine writing a college term paper so undeniably correct that it overrules two centuries of legal precedent, amends the United States Constitution, and forces your university to retroactively change your grade from a 'C' to an 'A' ten years later. In 1982, Gregory Watson, a 19-year-old sophomore at the University of Texas at Austin, was researching a paper for his government class when he stumbled across an obscure piece of American history. One of the original twelve amendments drafted by James Madison in 1789 as part of the initial Bill of Rights had never actually been ratified by enough states. This specific proposal mandated that any pay raise voted on by members of Congress could not take effect until after an intervening election of Representatives had occurred, preventing politicians from instantly lining their own pockets.

While ten of Madison's proposals became the famous Bill of Rights in 1791, this pay-delay amendment languished in legal limbo. Because the original text possessed no built-in expiration date—unlike modern amendments which typically feature a strict seven-year deadline—Watson posited a bold legal thesis: the amendment was still technically live and legally eligible for ratification by state legislatures across the country.

Watson's professor was entirely unimpressed by the unconventional argument, handing the paper a mediocre grade of 'C' and dismissing the concept as impossible. Refusing to accept defeat, Watson launched a relentless, self-funded one-man campaign. He began writing letters to state legislators nationwide, arguing that ratifying a 200-year-old amendment was not only constitutionally valid under Article V, but also a crucial mechanism for legislative accountability.

His campaign gained massive momentum during a period of intense public frustration over Congressional compensation. State after state began voting to ratify the dormant text. Finally, on May 7, 1992, Michigan became the 38th state to approve the measure, fulfilling the required three-fourths majority dictated by the Constitution. Archivist of the United States Don W. Wilson officially certified the proposal as the 27th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution. It remains the most recent amendment added to the nation's founding document. Decades after giving the initial 'C', the university officially changed Watson’s paper grade to an 'A', immortalizing one of the greatest academic revenge stories in constitutional history.
